title: Beyond Prompting: Context Engineering for Production-Grade AI
gist: Redis developer advocate Ricardo Ferreira walks through building an Alexa skill ('My Jarvis') on the open-source Redis Agent Memory Server, LangChain4j and OpenAI under a hard 8-second Alexa timeout, and shows that neither upgrading the model nor writing better system prompts fixed context failures — only deliberate techniques did: tools for time, session memory with TTL, HNSW vector search with post-filtering for multi-tenancy, query compression, few-shot behavioral hints, Cohere reranking at an 80% minimum score, token-window trimming, LLM summarization, and semantic caching. His central warning is that context engineering silently multiplies LLM calls and turns cost from linear into exponential.

themes.theme: The false fixes: bigger models and better prompts

insights.claim: Upgrading to a newer, larger-context model increased cost and did nothing to fix a degraded conversational AI experience — the reflex to scale the backend, borrowed from on-prem database tuning, does not transfer to context failures.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Model-upgrade spend is often wasted on problems that are architectural; scrutinize AI budget lines that assume a bigger model solves quality issues.
insights.quote: not all the time, upgrading to newer models in your AI implementation is going to solve your problems. I know for sure that in my case, it didn't solve mine.
insights.locator: Using Newer Models as a Solution

insights.claim: Writing a more elaborate system prompt to make the agent 'think clearer' was explicitly a mistake; the fix required a series of intentional, individually engineered mechanisms rather than better prompting.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Prompt-only vendors and internal 'prompt library' efforts address a narrow slice of the real failure surface.
insights.quote: let me create a more elaborated system prompt that would help the agent to think a little clearer and better. Another mistake.
insights.locator: Agents Need Context

insights.claim: Context engineering is defined operationally as a set of very intentional, well-crafted approaches that pragmatically solve each specific bad experience, going beyond prompting.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Gives a testable definition — ask which specific failure each technique addresses, rather than accepting 'context engineering' as a marketing label.
insights.locator: Agents Need Context

insights.claim: For any serious AI implementation providing human-like experiences, context engineering has become part of the architecture rather than an optional feature, and should be designed proactively instead of retrofitted reactively.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Teams treating context engineering as a later optimization will repeatedly rework their architecture — a hidden schedule risk in AI product plans.
insights.quote: I did the reactive mode, but I could have been proactive.
insights.locator: Final Note on Context Engineering

insights.claim: Context failures in conversational agents fall into distinct named categories: context poisoning (nonsense entering the context), context distraction (too much irrelevant data slowing and degrading answers), context confusion (mixed irrelevant data), context rot as context grows, and context clash (contradictory true/false and versioned facts colliding).
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: A diagnostic taxonomy for triaging agent quality complaints — each failure class maps to a different remediation and a different vendor category.
insights.locator: Different Types of Context Problems

insights.claim: Once an LLM call is made, retrieving an answer is easy — the difficulty is the human aspect and mannerisms of interaction, which is where most of the engineering effort actually goes.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Demo-to-production gap in conversational AI is almost entirely interaction quality, not answer generation — discount demos accordingly.
insights.quote: the skill was able to retrieve answers, but it's fairly easy. Once you actually make a call to the LLMs, it's going to be virtually able to respond to any possible question.
insights.locator: Different Types of Context Problems

insights.claim: LLMs have no reliable concept of the current date and time, which had to be solved by giving the model a tool that supplies date and time context — a prerequisite for any reminder or scheduling use case.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Temporal grounding via tools is a mandatory first build step for scheduling agents — a common source of silent wrong answers when omitted.
insights.locator: Chapter 1: Pragmatically Solving Each Problem

themes.theme: Memory architecture: short-term, long-term, knowledge bases

insights.claim: Because LLMs are stateless, a session-bounded short-term memory with a TTL is required; a five-minute TTL was chosen as adequate for recalling the immediately preceding conversation, after which the agent legitimately forgets.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: TTL choice directly trades storage and token cost against perceived continuity — a tunable lever with visible product consequences.
insights.locator: Another incidental realization was LLMs are stateless

insights.claim: The framework's built-in chat memory implementation malfunctioned because LLMs make bi-directional calls between tools, causing a forever loop of tool invocations that pushed response time past ten seconds and broke a hard eight-second timeout.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Off-the-shelf memory abstractions can fail catastrophically under tool-calling loops — a latency risk to test explicitly before committing to a framework.
insights.locator: One of the things that I realized with this

insights.claim: The fix was replacing the buffered chat memory with a custom pass-through implementation that solved both the tool-call loop and cross-call conversation persistence at once — but at the cost of a forever-growing context.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: This exact trade — fixing a latency bug by removing the memory cap — is what later produced exponential token cost; watch for it in your own stack.
insights.locator: I had to replace it with my own implementation

insights.claim: The memory service uses an LLM in the background to promote short-term session memories into long-term memories automatically as conversations continue, rather than requiring explicit persistence calls.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Background LLM promotion is invisible token spend — a cost line teams routinely fail to budget for.
insights.locator: This is the Redis Agent Memory Architecture

insights.claim: Long-term memory retrieval is implemented as a RAG-style ContentRetriever performing semantic vector search with an HNSW index, chosen as highly efficient at scale and not memory hungry, returning top-k results.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: HNSW plus top-k is the default retrieval configuration; index choice and k are the two knobs that most affect both cost and answer quality.
insights.locator: The way you implement this in LangChain4j

insights.claim: A separate category of long-term memory — a knowledge base built from documents rather than conversational memories — required a second retriever plus an LLM-powered query router that decides per question whether to hit user memories or the knowledge base.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Routing is itself an inline LLM call before the answering call — each retrieval sophistication adds a billable round trip.
insights.locator: I ended up creating something that I called knowledge bases

insights.claim: Choosing the right top-k value for memory retrieval is an unresolved empirical question — how many memories are enough to formulate a correct answer has no principled answer and was tuned by hand.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Manual hyperparameter tuning of retrieval remains a hidden operational burden — an opening for tooling that automates it.
insights.locator: Secondly, probably this is going to be a very simple thing

insights.claim: Once multiple household members used the same agent, multi-tenancy had to be enforced with vector search post-filtering — retrieve results by similarity, then filter on metadata such as tenant ID and owner ID — because otherwise one user's questions could be answered from another user's memories.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Cross-tenant memory leakage is a concrete privacy failure mode in agent products; post-filtering is the minimum control and should be an audit item.
insights.locator: I had to figure out a way to use multi-tenancy

insights.claim: Vector search is not exact search, so a question about a 'favorite' pulled back both favorite color and favorite programming language, and the LLM correctly but unhelpfully answered with all of it — the model is not at fault, the retrieval design is.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Over-answering is a retrieval-precision failure misdiagnosed as a model failure — the wrong diagnosis leads to the wrong (expensive) fix.
insights.quote: Vector search is not an exact search. The name tells everything.
insights.locator: Can you guess why he did answer that

insights.claim: Pronoun and reference resolution across turns was solved with query compression via a query transformer, using the LLM to substitute references on the fly so a follow-up like 'where does he live' resolves to the previously named person.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Compression is a cheap, high-impact technique for conversational agents and another pre-flight LLM call to account for in cost models.
insights.quote: Compression is another technique of context engineering that for a human being, it would be so natural, but you have to teach those things when you interact with your AI services.
insights.locator: In LangChain4j terms, you use a tech

insights.claim: Few-shot design — supplying positive, negative and contradictory examples in a structured system prompt — was used as behavioral rather than cognitive engineering, teaching the model how to behave and not just what to think; roughly 17 examples were built for the original implementation.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Few-shot behavioral hints delivered measurably more objective answers where prompt rewriting alone had failed — a low-cost lever before reaching for reranking.
insights.quote: It's more like a behavioral engineering type of thing, the use of few-shots.
insights.locator: it's a technique called few-shots design

themes.theme: Reranking, model choice and calibration fragility

insights.claim: Reranking was needed because multiple retrieved memories can all be correct yet differ in priority, and the LLM must be taught relative importance; it was implemented with a scoring model wired into a content aggregator that reranks top-k vector results at a manually calibrated 80% minimum score, all in pre-flight before the answering LLM call.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Reranking thresholds are hand-calibrated magic numbers in production systems — a fragility and maintenance cost buyers should probe.
insights.locator: the technique for the context engineering that I ended up using was reranking

insights.claim: Cohere was selected for reranking as, at the time, the only open LLM model supporting reranking with an API, and it was described as working very well and being super cheap.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Cohere holds a defensible niche in reranking distinct from the frontier-model race — a differentiated revenue line worth tracking.
insights.locator: In this case, I used Cohere

insights.claim: The choice of a hosted reranker was forced by infrastructure limits, not preference: an AWS Lambda JAR is capped at 50 megabytes for direct upload and 250 megabytes via S3, and bundling a self-deployed ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6 ONNX reranking model produced a JAR twice the supported size, whereas the Cohere API dependency kept it under about 100 megabytes.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Serverless packaging limits push teams from self-hosted models to paid inference APIs — a structural, under-appreciated driver of API revenue.
insights.locator: Two lessons learned about this exercise

insights.claim: Changing the underlying model directly invalidates the calibration of the reranking minimum score — the 80% threshold tuned for one model did not work with another, meaning solved issues systematically reopen whenever someone swaps models.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Model portability is far lower in practice than 'model-agnostic' marketing implies; every swap carries a hidden recalibration cost.
insights.quote: That's the type of thing that will happen systematically.
insights.locator: Also, something that I've noticed as well

themes.theme: Cost: from linear to exponential, and back to flat

insights.claim: Solving context problems systematically meant using the LLM more and more for purposes other than answering the question — routing, compression, summarization — so context engineering carries an incidental but material cost that is the single biggest heads-up for anyone adopting it.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Auxiliary LLM calls, not the user-facing call, drive AI unit economics — model cost forecasts built on one call per query will be badly wrong.
insights.locator: Chapter 2: Dealing with the Monthly Cost

insights.claim: At a measured baseline of three household users at roughly 10 queries per day each, LLM cost was a flat $4.20 per family with reranking via Cohere under a dollar — small in absolute terms but structurally alarming when extrapolated to scale.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Concrete per-user AI cost anchors for consumer assistant workloads — useful for sanity-checking any consumer AI business model.
insights.locator: The average number of queries

insights.claim: With a forever-growing pass-through context, cost growth was exponential rather than linear because every LLM tool-calling round trip appends to the same JSON payload, driving token consumption far higher than query volume alone would suggest.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Tool-heavy agents have superlinear cost curves — the key reason agent pilots look cheap and production deployments do not.
insights.quote: The context growth exactly different from the LLM cost and the Cohere cost for reranking was not linear, was exponential, because the context kept growing for every single interaction.
insights.locator: Now let me remind you of a mistake

insights.claim: The stated cost objective for production AI systems is constant time — flat, fixed cost per interaction — rather than accepting growth that scales with conversation length.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Flat per-interaction cost is the design target to demand from any agent architecture proposal.
insights.quote: What we want is constant time. We want flat and constant time, fixed cost.
insights.locator: At scale, that would become a very serious problem

insights.claim: Token-window chat memory caps context at a model's maximum token count — 4,096 for the GPT-3.5 generation used — and trims by tokens rather than message count, but requires a model-specific token count estimator because tokenization and payload structure differ between providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Provider-specific token accounting is another concrete switching cost undermining model-agnostic claims.
insights.quote: The strategy of counting varies for every specific model.
insights.locator: There's a built-in implementation, a LangChain4j

insights.claim: Naive token-window trimming keeps cost flat but loses context, because the built-in rule deletes whatever is oldest regardless of whether an old message was highly relevant to the conversation.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Cost control and answer quality are in direct tension in agent memory; naive trimming trades one for the other invisibly.
insights.locator: However, what is the problem that actually started happening

insights.claim: Summarization replaced arbitrary trimming: a custom chat memory makes an additional LLM call to extract and summarize everything relevant — facts, preferences, strong statements — so messages are deleted consciously rather than arbitrarily while keeping cost flat.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Paying for a summarization call to avoid unbounded context is the standard flat-cost pattern — budget the summarizer as a fixed overhead per session.
insights.quote: It has to delete message consciously at very best.
insights.locator: Recently, I use another technique also from context engineering called summarization

insights.claim: Semantic caching differs from conventional caching by evaluating the semantic meaning of a query rather than doing an exact key lookup, so two differently worded questions with the same meaning must produce a cache hit rather than a miss.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Semantic caching is the clearest direct lever on LLM API spend — evaluate it before negotiating volume pricing.
insights.locator: I started using semantic caching

insights.claim: Semantic caching cut redundant LLM calls substantially in a household assistant workload, with the speaker reporting he reduced most of the 75% of his redundant calls in more than half.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: A large fraction of real assistant traffic is semantically redundant — a structural argument that inference demand is softer than raw query counts imply.
insights.quote: I reduced most of the 75% of my redundant calls in more than half, which is good.
insights.locator: It solved the problem

insights.claim: The danger of semantic caching is false hits: small differences in wording, or a non-native accent producing unusual transcriptions, can trigger a cache hit that returns the wrong answer instead of calling the LLM, so the similarity threshold must be continuously calibrated.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Semantic cache false hits are a silent correctness risk that scales with accent and dialect diversity — an accessibility and quality liability in global deployments.
insights.locator: The negative part is that sometimes

insights.claim: Semantic caching is structurally just the cache-aside pattern with vector similarity replacing exact key lookup — go to the cache, and if the answer is not there, go to the LLM.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Familiar caching architecture means the engineering lift is low; adoption barriers are calibration and trust, not complexity.
insights.locator: How many of you can tell me what is the name of this pattern

insights.claim: A fixed 8-second Alexa interaction timeout was the hard constraint that made this workload a genuine stress test of an agent memory layer and forced every latency decision in the system.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Voice platform timeouts, not model speed, set the real latency budget for consumer voice AI — they cap how much pre-flight context work is affordable.
insights.locator: Initial Implementation

insights.claim: The final pipeline stacks four pre-flight stages before the answering LLM call — a context injector for few-shots, a query transformer for compression, a query router choosing between knowledge base and long-term memories, and a content aggregator performing reranking — up from an initial assumption that the LLM would simply answer the question.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Four pre-flight stages is the realistic complexity of a production conversational agent — a useful yardstick for sizing build effort and latency budget.
insights.quote: Again, it all started with a simple assumption, I just want the LLM to answer the questions.
insights.locator: Then you start seeing this, that my pipeline execution

insights.claim: The stack was deliberately Java-based — an AWS Lambda backend, the Alexa Skills SDK, and LangChain4j calling OpenAI on top of Redis — showing production agent work is not confined to Python tooling.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: Enterprise Java agent frameworks are viable and reduce the retraining cost of AI adoption for large JVM shops.
insights.locator: Initial Implementation

insights.claim: The conclusion of the internal stress test was that the Redis-based Agent Memory Server was suitable for human-interaction workloads, with virtually everything that needed fixing lying outside the memory server itself.
insights.speaker: Ricardo Ferreira
insights.so_what: The memory store is not the bottleneck in agent quality — spend and scrutiny belong in the orchestration layer above it.
insights.locator: Chapter 2: Dealing with the Monthly Cost
